utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleague Mr. Williamson and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Toma Fila and I appear with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic as the Defence for Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? Thank you. All right. I understand you have called a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, just a brief preliminary matter before that. We have completed the preliminary list of witnesses that we intend to call for next week, and we have also included the statement of a witness Dzuka Radici which was the only statement, I believe, which your Honours had not received previously in relation to witnesses to be called next week. I have already provided copies of both of these documents to the Defence, and in the course of the morning I will be providing a Croatian translation of this statement to the Defence as well. But at this time I can give these to the usher and they can be presented to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you going to call only seven witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears at this time that that is all that we are going to have available. We are still in the process of working on this issue, but there may be one additional witness other than that, but right now I believe that is all that we have, and we would then be prepared when we return in March to present all of the evidence in regard to the exhumation and a couple of other witnesses. And that should be the end of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you think we can finish in March?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: With the Prosecution case, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. Now, as you know, in March, we only have, I think, five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There will be relatively few witnesses in March, although the witnesses that will be testifying, I think, some of their testimony will be fairly lengthy because it deals with some technical issues and again the results of the exhumation, but it is our belief that we should be able to finish our case in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when do you think you may be able to interview the 45 defence witnesses in Belgrade? Remember, we agreed that you would try to interview them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be our intention to do that in the break between the February and March sessions, so we should be in a position in March to notify the court and the Defence of which witnesses upon which we have reached agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excellent. So in theory, in April, we could start with the Defence witnesses. Yes? Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, the Defence will not have a single question for any of the witnesses we are hearing today, but I would like you to convey on behalf of the Defence our condolences for their losses in this unfortunate war. Regarding the Ovcara questions, the Defence is not denying at all the findings there and that those people were killed at Ovcara. I said yesterday too, and last time, that I am not disputing that there was an armed conflict. What I am disputing is an international armed conflict. I am not disputing that there were 200 bodies found. I am just trying to establish which bodies they were. Therefore, things will proceed very expeditiously as far as I am concerned. And a last point, I should like to make; I have agreed with the Prosecution, in yesterday's statement of Mr. Cakalic it is stated that he was shown a photograph of the accused, Dokmanovic, wearing a camouflage uniform. Through the kindness of the Prosecution I will be shown the photographs. I wish to draw the attention of the court to the fact that those photographs need to be seen for us to establish whether that was an uniform or the kind of clothing that I showed you here at a closed session, if you recall, that we had once. That is all I had to say and I will be of no further bother to the court until the end of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You do not bother the court, you help the court, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could point out one other small factor in relation to the witness list that I have provided, the last witness that is indicated on that list, Mr. Peter Kiper is a Czech diplomat who was an ECMM monitor at the time of the conflict in Yugoslavia. He will be testifying on Wednesday, 11th, and he has requested to be able to testify in the Czech language so we have made arrangements for interpreters who are having to be brought from another country so we had to specify an exact date on which he would testify and we have stated that for the 11th, so if we finish with the other witnesses prior to that, it still would be necessary to reconvene on the 11th to hear his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If your Honours please, I can proceed with the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you state your name for the record, please? I am sorry, I do not believe the witness has made the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask the witness to make the solemn declaration? VEBER, LEOPOLD VLADIMIR (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Veber, Leopold Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, where are you from originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long has your family been in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family has been in Vukovar to the best of my knowledge since the days of my father. My father was born in 1915, and according to the book of births, my grandfather, Anton, was also born in Vukovar, so that is all I know. I do not know exactly what year my grandfather was born in but both my grandfather and my father were born in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And until 1991 was your whole life spent in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I spent my entire life in Vukovar. I completed my apprenticeship there in 1958. I am a hairdresser, so that is also where I finished elementary school and this secondary school for hairdressing and then I worked in Bor for some time, for some years, that is a hairdressing salon, and in 1964 I went to Vukovar and I opened a hairdressing salon for women, one of my own, and I worked there until 1985, until 31st December 1985. Then I re-trained to do something else. I closed down the shop for justified reasons, and I passed the necessary exams in order to be in charge of central heating because in the town of Vukovar a home for the elderly was opened. At that time it was called, "the home of veterans and retirees". They needed a person who would be in charge of central heating. I got this job, so in 1986, on 1st October, I got this job and until the outbreak of the war I worked in that home for retired persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had two children. I had a daughter who was born in 1967 and a son who was killed during the war. He was born in 1969. I only had the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your son's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son's name was Veber, Sinisa. He was born on 22nd February 1969.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son Sinisa attend school in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My son completed elementary school in Vukovar, and then he enrolled in secondary school, and he completed it, thus becoming I would call a "tjrol" technician at Pik, Vukovar. He finished his apprenticeship but he did not get a job because he went to the army and then he came back from the army, he did not have a job, so he went to Verona, to Italy to work for a spell with someone from Borovo, a painter, an artist. He was selling paintings there, so he worked there for about two months, and then he came back for some kind of vacation, just before the war broke out, and he sent another colleague to go there and he said that he would be coming back to continue, but then he did not. He stayed on in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As your son was growing up and as a young man, was he involved in any kind of sports activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sinisa was involved in sports. He rowed, and I cannot tell you exactly what year he started to row. I do not know exactly. When he was very young, and he rowed in the Vukovar club. Their young team achieved some very good results. He rowed in eight- and four-member teams. These young people were so good, and they were even better than their older fellow sportsmen, and at a championship that was held in Vukovar the president of the club said that that had never happened before, that such a young team of rowers would win the title even before the championship actually began. They were better than the older team. So, the ex-champions from Zadar were defeated, so the Vukovar club became the champions. I know that this man said -- the diploma went into the hands of the sweet ones from the salty ones, you see. They lived on the banks of the River Danube and Zadar is on the banks of the Adriatic coast by the sea. So, before the war, before the army, he actually went to the army in 1978. He went to the army in 1978, and before that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, if I can interrupt you for a moment, are you saying he went to the army in 1978? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, 1988. 1988. Oh, you see... 1989, yes, yes. I got carried away. In 1989, in February 1989 he came back from the army, that is to say that he went to the army in 1988. That is to say that he had won all those medals before the war, before he went to the army. So six years before that they were the champions of then Yugoslavia, of the entire country. They were the only team consisting of eight young men to have won the title in that way. All eight of them belonged to the same club and they were champions, and also for three times they won the European championship, that is to say that twice they defended their European championship title.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veber, if I can stop you at that point, I would like at this point to show you a photograph and if you can tell me who is portrayed in this photograph, please, and we will mark this as Prosecutor's exhibit...

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: 59. Can you tell the court who is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this point I would like to tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 59.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is all right. It was not a question for you. In 1991 did your son suggest to you that maybe you should leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My son suggested that his mother and I and sister leave Vukovar, because I worked in this home for the elderly. From May 1st I was mobilised with the civilian defence, and I was supposed to stay at that home only during the night, because most of the other staff members were women and they were afraid to be on their own so I could not leave the place because of that. They told me that I could even spend the night there, that I would be paid a special bonus because a nurse would be there on night duty and she would -- she was afraid of being on her own and she did not feel safe, so...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sinisa also stay in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Sinisa also stayed in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he join in the defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He joined the defence of the city. Also through these local communes, as the place was organised then, and they were all supposed to go on duty, as it was called then, so he stayed on in our local community which was called Vladimir Nazor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any idea what his responsibilities were with the defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His duties? I do not know exactly what he was. I do not know but it was like I know that he had night duty, and that he would come back. Since I was at this other place we would see each other from time to time. I do not know. Until August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of the home for the elderly where you were working during the course of the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions there were very difficult because there were quite a few people there who were immobile, who were handicapped, and there were about 120 people staying there. The situation was such that there was hardly any electric supply because of the shelling of Vukovar and there was no water. The home was shot at quite a lot and we were among the first to have casualties among these old people who were incapable of going downstairs. There was not a proper shelter there, though. I do not know what kind of arms these were, were they launchers or mortars or cannons, but it was a new building and everything was bursting all over the place. There was no heating, and when this first attack occurred, we had two or three dead and seven or eight wounded people, and Radio Vukovar had broadcast that, that the home for the elderly was shelled, and that there were casualties there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veber, was the home for the elderly used for any kind of military purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The home for the elderly was such that there were only civilian people there when we did not have any water, then they would come and bring us water because these people did not have any drinking water, and I had a boiler room downstairs for heating where there were about 3,000 litres for heating, so I opened that, so that we could use this water for washing our faces and we used it for the toilet, so that is it. So, the army would only come after the shelling. They would come very quickly to give aid to the wounded and take them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veber, where was your house located in Vukovar? Which section of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house was near the water tower, near, in Slavija, a mill. It was the first electric mill after the Second World War. I do not know. It is about 500 metres away from the water tower. That is to say, close to Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time as the battle was coming to a close did you leave your home and go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not leave our home because I was up there all the time, and my mother and my aunt and some other neighbours who were elderly, since we had a good basement, stayed at home quite a lot. I do not know, until...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I was talking about near the end of the battle. At some point in time did you, in fact, leave and move to someplace else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We left the house. I was up there at Mitnica and my family was taken to the shelter. My mother and my sister had to -- to the centre of town near the bus station, there is a shelter there, and that is where they were until the very fall of Vukovar and I was at Mitnica, together with a few of these women because before this shelling we managed to evacuate half of these people who were badly wounded and who were mobile anyway and we were supposed to evacuate the remaining 60 persons too but it was not safe any longer so I had to stay until the very end, together with these old people up there in this home for retirees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the end my Sinisa was at the hospital because he was wounded, and before that he was not even wounded and he was in the centre of town and he went up there to see me and we went to Olajnica and we spent a few days there. We were there a few days before Vukovar fell. He was wounded then. He was in hospital because he had a concussion, and he was not wounded by the actual bullet, but from the pebbles and rocks that hit him as a result of this shell that had fallen. He could not hear very well and in the hospital when he heard about this evacuation he came to pick me up. It was a Sunday. It was the 17th -- between the 17th and the 18th, so it was already around 12.30, the beginning of the 18th, Monday. I know that it was raining, and we went to the hospital. That is where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you accommodated at the hospital? Where did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came there we entered the hallway. It is a big hallway and there were a lot of civilians there. We were in a hallway first and then we went to this other place where these other people were, and we found ourselves a small space there and that is where we sat until the morning. The next day we walked around a bit. This was the 19th by then, yes, yes, it was the 19th because Monday was the 18th. So I was there. I did not leave that place. This is the very entrance to the hospital. I mean, not into the compound, the yard, but into the building itself. Upstairs the shelling had damaged the building quite a bit but downstairs it was all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Sinisa staying with you in the same place in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sinisa was there with the other wounded. He came to see us a couple of times to see how we were. It was a short period of time. It was Monday, and then Tuesday I was with him at 12.30. I saw him. We kissed each other, and they had already started leaving that day. It was Tuesday, and he said, "see you in Zagreb", and I said, "are you coming with us?", and he said, "no, I have my own company here and I was staying with them here so I will stay on with them", so my wife was there too, and she said, "I was with Sinisa now", and I said, "I saw him at 12.30", so I was with him at 12.30. My wife saw him about an hour and a half later, and after that the room was emptied. These buses came that took them to Velepromet. I was among the last, perhaps, to leave. My wife and I, that is, and they returned us a few times. The army was all around, tanks were there, they were saying, "you are going", "you are not going". All the buses had left, and I cannot tell exactly how many of us stayed on, not too many, about 20, all of us civilians. Then they say, "you are leaving". So then we got out and some kind of a military truck came, not the big one, a wide one. I do not know what it is called. I cannot remember the vehicle, but I just know it was a military vehicle, grey, olive green, and a soldier gave us some hot tea, a piece of bread, and a can, and we took it with us. We entered the vehicle, and we went up there towards the military barracks. We reached the barracks before dark. I was not looking at my watch. I did not know what time it was, so we were in front of Velepromet for some time, and it was getting dark and then they turned the war lights on, you know, the lights on the car that are not really glaring lights, but the ones they put down, so we got out, and they put us someplace on the right-hand side. We were waiting there, I do not know how long, but quite long, and we waited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was on the 19th that you were taken from the hospital to Velepromet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your son Sinisa remained at the hospital at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sinisa stayed at the hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so this was the last time that you had seen him, was this occasion at 12.30. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the last time I saw him, yes, the last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he have with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sinisa had a small bag and in it he had his passport, he had those medals that he had won, his rowing medals, exactly 38 medals. Obviously he was so pleased that he took them along with him. He also had some underwear, and I do not know what else. Some very small things. It was a very light bag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long were you held at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Velepromet that evening when we arrived we stayed there for quite a long time. It was night-time, and it gets dark early and I was not really looking at my watch, and I just know when we came we were told to stand there, not to go anywhere. This was in the yard, two APCs got in. They had their lights on. They turned around, towards the exit of Velepromet. They turned on these lights and they were actually lighting the exit. I do not know those people. I do not know who those people were, if you were to ask me now I have no idea. I stayed there because a captain told me that I should not move and I was standing there, and a bus was supposed to come and -- in front of these APCs, and it stood there. Boys were passing by, men, two by two in pairs, their hands were tied to one another, and they were boarding the bus and when the bus was full then it left Velepromet and went out to the main road. Then another bus came and I cannot say exactly when, but I think there were eight buses for sure, perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veber, if I can stop you right there, what was going on at Velepromet on the day of the 20th, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 20th I remember exactly. It was a Wednesday. My wife and I and the rest of us who had spent the night in the carpenter's shop there, someone said to us, I do not know what rank he had, he was a reservist, to go out. And we stood there, and my wife, because my mother, sister and daughter were also in Velepromet and they were in a bus that was about to leave, and then my wife went over to give them some addresses. At that moment, when she left, I stayed behind alone. Somebody I had never seen before came up to me wearing an olive green uniform, asking, "who is Vader Veber", and I said, "I am", and he said, "come here". So I asked someone next to me to look over this little bag. We also had a few of our personal things, underwear and that sort of thing in it. Then he said, "Well, come here", and he started pushing me. Then I was going back again to this carpenter shop. It was not a big hall, it was a place where the woodworking was done. Then there were three persons, also people I did not know. One of them was very tall and strong, and he said, "give me that MUP number". I was never in MUP. When I got in I had to spread out my arms and my legs. I had a winter wind breaker on me. He took it off. He threw it away, to the side. He searched me in case I had any weapons. He did not find anything. He opened the door, and he shoved me inside. There was a room to the left, and another one to the right. I entered the one in the middle. That morning I was in the right one, and then he moved me to the left one, so I fell over some other people. I saw the faces, they were all scared. I recognised quite a number of people. We kept quiet. We stayed there from Tuesday, that was -- you said the 20th -- no, no, that was Wednesday, was it not? The 20th was a Wednesday. And I stayed there until the 21st, the Thursday, in the evening, about 9.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Veber, on the 21st, did you have a chance to meet up with some other people who indicated to you that they had come from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not there but in Mitrovica, when we were in Mitrovica, two persons, and another one later on, that we happened to get together. Actually they were in Velepromet as well, and they told me that my son had ended up in Ovcara. Actually, that they had seen my son in Ovcara, so I asked how did they know, and then they said that somebody had taken them out of there, they had known my son and they had seen him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were in Mitrovica. When did you go to Mitrovica? What was the date, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening, Thursday evening, I knew the ranks well. I do not know the new ones. He was captain, first class. He came in. There were just a few of us left inside in this kind of -- probably a small warehouse, storage room, and he came in, and he said, "come on quickly if, we manage to save you". There was a bus outside, and he could not get it started, so he asked us to push it. I was just wearing my jogging suit and he said, "Well, have you not got anything else?", and I said, "no"; "Well, how could you have come just wearing that", and then I told him that someone had taken it off me and thrown it away. Then he found a pullover for me. He gave it to me, I put it on, on top of my jogging suit, because it was rather cold. I was shivering. There was no heating, so we went out into the yard. There was a drizzle. This was Thursday evening, 21st, or was it the 22nd? No, the 21st, no, the 21st in the evening, a Thursday. So we pushed this bus, it got started. We jumped onto it quickly, the driver and this captain, and they transported us from Velepromet. They did not even switch on the lights. This was during the night, and they took us to the Vukovar barracks where we got out, and again, after those two days, they gave us -- we were thirsty, they gave us water and we were hungry. We were given another can of food and half a loaf of bread they gave us. So we ate that, we drank some water. We were given a packet of cigarettes each for two days we did not have any, and then they listed us, and on Friday, so that means the 22nd in the morning, they transferred us to Mitrovica which means that on Friday 22nd I was in Mitrovica. Not just me, but a busload of us. More than 30. We could not count, but there were more than 30 people inside. I know there are that many seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not familiar with Mitrovica. They said we were at the -- at the prison and we were in the bus outside. We were not allowed to go out and we waited. We did not know what we were waiting for, but they said they had to wait for the interrogation that we would be interviewed, and then released home. I cannot remember what time it was. I know that some people were passing by. They were spitting at the windows, saying, "those are Ustashas inside". Then one of the officers inside told us not to react, just to bend our heads and not to get upset about it. Then we went inside the bus. All of us got off. There was a large yard with high walls. We were lined up there against the wall with our hands up, facing the wall, and we heard someone behind us, "target -- aim", and then I wondered why had they brought us all this way and wasted so much fuel? There were two buses and there were two APCs escorting us, probably to protect us, one in front of the bus and one behind us, when we were being taken from Vukovar to Mitrovica, and there we were standing facing the wall, hearing this order, "aim", and we were waiting for them to fire. However, no one did. One of ours turned around, and somebody hit him on the head saying, "what are you turning around for?", but he wanted to see whether they were going to fire or not. So we stood there. Nobody fired, then we turned around, and I saw that there were quite a number of them. I do not know how many, but they no longer had olive green uniforms, but the blue police uniforms, the uniform of the policemen in the former Yugoslavia was. We used to call them, "the blue ones". Then we were passing from that yard into another. They were standing on both sides. We passed between them, they hit us with the batons, some people on the head, some people on the stomach. We had to run through. It depended how quickly one passed to avoid the blows. And then we entered a hall, a sports hall like a gym. We had a take all our clothes off, absolutely, we had to strip, they examined us to make sure, whether we had any weapons or I do not know what else, then we put back on our clothes again, then we went out. We all had to lie down, and we lay there. I do not know for how long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veber, if I could stop you now, where is Sremska Mitrovica located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sremska Mitrovica is when you are going from Vukovar, you would go to Sid, as far as I remember you follow the highway and then you turn to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is in the Republic of Serbia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is. It is situated in the Republic of Serbia, yes, because Sid, too was all part of Serbia. In fact, I think they had the same licence plates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you met up with some of the people that had been at Ovcara. This was in Sremska Mitrovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people from Vukovar, to your knowledge, were held at this prison in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many people. For a long time we did not know how many there were until a list was made at the International Red Cross that was visiting, gave us some of these lists and according to those lists, we learned that more than 1,000, I think it was 1,200 people were there in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people civilians, soldiers or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, they were all in civilian clothes, the people I saw, with the exception of a couple of them who had stayed behind wearing a police uniform. A couple of them that I knew I saw in the cell that I was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Cakalic also held in this prison with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say for sure. I arrived on the 22nd. That morning when I arrived they brought I do not know how many more people, and among them was Cakalic. I remember that. Drago Berghofer on that same day, that must have been, I suppose, 21st, the Wednesday. And I remember also Ljubo Vagar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is all right, Mr. Veber. Was there one occasion when Mr. Cakalic assisted you and you felt like, in effect, he had saved your life when you were at this prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As he was taken out of Vukovar at the same time as me, he also was taken to the barracks. We were transported together to Sremska Mitrovica. He was also badly beaten, like me, only they had a little more clothing, so the blows did not hurt them so badly, because after all those beatings, I did not tell you everything that the blue ones did to us. It was dark already, and we were so exhausted that we could no longer stand, and they told us to go to what we learned was the third pavilion in Mitrovica, so I went. I was the first or the second, I cannot remember, among the first, and Cakalic was behind me. We reached the second floor. I remember that. I entered this corridor, and then I felt something bursting in my head, so then after that I do not know what happened, but I know that when I came to I was lying on my back looking up and I saw faces looking at me, saying, "he has come to. He is better". So they gave me water, they lifted me up. I recognised one of them. I thought his name was Bozo but it is not, it is Ante. He used to work in Pik. I saw him, so I even thought that he belonged to their army. I did not know where I was because I was surrounded and they were looking at me, and I said, "Bozo, what have I done to anyone to be beaten like this?", and he said, "now calm down. It will be all right", and then when I calmed down a bit I said, "where am I?", and he said, "Well, you know where you are, here we are", but I was rather lost and then I realised that those were my people from Vukovar because some people were already there before we arrived. Half the bus came to this particular room. Others were distributed to other rooms, and then I saw that Emil was there, Ljubo Vagar in that cell -- one could call it a cell, probably, what else -- then they lifted me up. I could not stand because I had been kicked in the backbone and in the neck. My nose was broken, some people did not even recognise me, people who knew me well, so they took me to wash up a bit. Then Drago Berghofer came up to me and they did everything to revive me, and they told me that they had seen my son at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other discussions with them, with Mr. Berghofer, Mr. Cakalic about what had gone on at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked a little. They did not know much, or they did not want to tell me. I do not know. Judging by what Emil said, and Drago Berghofer who had been there, I saw that something was wrong. However, someone else, I do not know how he got there, he told me too that he had been at Ovcara. He comes from Sotin. That somebody he knew and who was wearing the other side's uniform, they were distributing people into groups, and he said that he was put in a group to wait. However, I thought that that was not a good place to be, so I moved to this other group, and then again he saw me in this other group and he ordered me to go back, and this happened three times. He tried a fourth time to move to this other group and he stayed alive. He does not know what happened to those others in the other group. So how he got out with some civilians, or whether somebody had saved him, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time you were eventually released from the prison in Sremska Mitrovica, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It occurred on the 27th March 1992. 27th March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were held in Mitrovica were you ever charged with any crimes or told that you were being held because of the commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked how many people I had killed, but I was not charged with any offence. No. I was not charged at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you eventually left in March, where did you go at that time? Back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Croatia. We went to Zagreb in the Vinko Bek hall. We saw the situation was very bad there. They took us around the hospitals to examine us. They established the injuries we had, so I was sent to a couple of places because I had several blows on my head. My spine had been injured, my shoulder too had suffered a lot of blows. I could not move my arm, so that I was taken around by our people from one doctor to another. I was still really lost, so I could not get around on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in February of 1997 did you get some new information about Sinisa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Ever since I left people were asking me where Sinisa was, what happened to him. Some people even said they had seen him in Sremska Mitrovica in a bus, but they said they did not know which direction he went, whether the bus went towards Aleksinac, or Nis or Belgrade or Novi Sad, but apparently he was seen. One person told me that, that this person had enquired about my son. He came to visit me. (10.15 am) That was the first news I got, so I felt consoled, "thank God, that he managed to survive Ovcara", because he asked me what was the last I had heard of my son and I said that he had been seen at Ovcara and I did not know what had happened to him. So when I got back from Mitrovica this person visited me at Vinko Bek. Whether he wanted to console me or something... Thank you, I was told that he was seen in Mitrovica so until last year I had hope that maybe he was captured somewhere, that he is working somewhere, because I heard from some other people that some people had been taken to Aleksinac, several buses of them, that only a couple of buses had gone to Nis, that they had selected the stronger ones and as he was strong, he was 1 metre 92 centimetres tall. You see? You can see how well-built he was, so I thought perhaps he was taken to the mine to work as a miner so I would prefer if he had been captured and he was working there, then if they kill him like that for nothing. So, until last year I had a shred of hope that he was alive. I gave his particulars to the International Red Cross, the national Red Cross, the descriptions, everything I knew concerning him. I went to enquire and they said, "as soon as we learn anything we will let you know",. I was notified last year in February, I cannot remember exactly the date, I think it was mid-February, when they exhumed the 200 bodies at Ovcara, as I had given a description, and on the basis of that description they saw it was Sinisa. First they notified me when I should report to the hospital. I cannot remember the name of the hospital. Salata, at Salata, at such and such an hour -- as my daughter was in Austria I informed her immediately so that my daughter and son-in-law came and my wife was with them because I had a little granddaughter, she was looking after her, and they came for the identification. When we got to Salata they took us to the room upstairs where the doctors, specialists for these things were. We were introduced and then according to our statements they asked us whether we accept or we do not accept. Then they showed us photographs for, after all, five years had gone by. So, you could only really see the bones, and then they brought a piece of pullover. It was greenish in colour. My wife noticed, although it was faded in colour by then, she recognised the pullover. That was one thing, and then the daughter knew which teeth had fillings, which were missing, and which had fillings, and the most important of all for identification, I think that they said that he must have been a very top quality athlete because of the muscles which were so well-developed, and this was seen from the bones, that only a really top-level sportsman could have such a body. What else? Oh yes. They asked us whether he had been wounded. No, he had a surface injury here. They were not real wounds that required any sewing up. And on his legs he had suffered a blow. Then my daughter remembered, "daddy, you know which leg that was". He had a motorbike as a young boy and he fell, and that was what they were able to notice on the bones. So there you are. We accepted that, and on the 7th March last year, he was buried at Mirogoj in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No questions? Mr. Veber, you heard before the kind words of the Defence counsel, Mr. Fila, who wished to express his human feelings of sorrow and regret for what happened to your son, and convey to you his condolences. Mr. Veber, the court is fully aware of the appalling ordeal you went through. On behalf of my colleagues and on my own behalf, I wish to express to you our full understanding for your plight, and our deep appreciation for your decision to come here to The Hague to testify before the International Criminal Tribunal. Thank you. Thank you so much. Are there any objections to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. The next witness will be Ljubica Dosen and she has not requested any kind of protection. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please make the formal declaration? LJUBICA DOSEN (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, from this witness we have an English version of the statement, and I believe that you have not yet received it -- oh, you have it. Oh, that is just perfect. Thank you very much. Good morning, Ms. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you feel comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interviewed by an investigator from this Tribunal on 22nd August 1995, and did you sign a document which was the English translation of that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show to you a document, and would like to ask you whether that was this very document which you have signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you see your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. It should be -- we have no Croatian version so far, and it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, but there is a misunderstanding. We got a translation into the Croatian language from the Prosecution, so there is a translation. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you very much. I will enquire and we will then tender it as Exhibit A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you again, Ms. Dosen, interviewed by an investigator from this Tribunal on 17th March 1996, and did you again sign a document which was the English translation of the second interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would also like to show you this document. I would like to ask you whether you again see your signature on the bottom of that document, on the pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would again like to tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 61 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, and I will look for the Croatian version as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we have not received this second document, the second interview taken on the 17th March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: At least I cannot find it. I have only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It might be attached to it. The first one has eight pages and then there is an additional three pages, but I would have three copies for you, your Honours, if you...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Defence has not received it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honours, for this inconvenience, and to the Defence as well, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Shall we give the Defence a few minutes so that they can go through the -- all right. Thank you. All right. So you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Will you please state to the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljubica Dosen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the place and date of your birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Luzani, Slavonski Brod, on 9th March 1949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a skilled worker and I make rubber footwear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it Vukovar your home town? Have you always been living in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Vukovar as a two-month baby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have most of your life been living in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All my life from then onwards. I lived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live in summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar, in the street of Mose Pijade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you live with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my husband, Martin Dosen and my daughter, Tanja Dosen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the profession of your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband is a fisherman, a private fisherman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he involved in politics? Was he a party member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was never involved in politics, but he was a member of the HD.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband also involved in the defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the reason why he was involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was involved in the defence of the town because the shelling had already started then and he simply wanted to protect his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your house also destroyed by shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was at the beginning, but it was not fully destroyed. It had only been shelled, because we were right next door to the theatre that was shelled very quickly and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband wounded in the course of the summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the events which led up to those wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband went to our then Territorial Defence to see what would happen and how they should be organised, and since those who were attacking us were on the other side of the Danube, and they knew where this was, and they shelled the Territorial Defence, and as he came in front of the Territorial Defence building, a shell fell and a fragment wounded his leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he treated in hospital because of these wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He stayed in the hospital and then he was sent home for treatment because he did not have to stay as an in-patient because it was only the leg tissue that was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he then again seriously wounded in November 1991 when he fell from the third floor balcony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he then again hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was then. He stayed on in the hospital. He did not come back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that? -- excuse me, I withdraw that. Did you and your daughter get the permission to join your husband to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Because my husband was immobile and he expressed his wish to have us with him so that I could help him because the staff was too busy with the other wounded people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join your husband? When did you move yourself into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband went to the hospital on November 16th, and we came between 17th and 18th to the hospital. I mean my daughter and I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many nights you did spend in the hospital alongside your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, two nights, and another day before the evacuation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you might have left the hospital either on the 19th or the 20th November. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the night of the 19th they came to the hospital, and we were evacuated on the morning of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us very briefly in general the overall situation in the hospital during these three, four days you stayed in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was terrible for me. First of all, there were very many wounded people, there was no water, there was no food, there was not any medicine. The shelling was very frequent. Civilians were coming in because they had nowhere else to go, because of all the shelling. You could feel blood everywhere. Doctor Bosanac feared an epidemic. There were people who were dying, they could not be buried because no one could go out because of the shelling. All of these people, really tormented. They did not have any cigarettes. They were hungry. They got some kind of food aid packages. They were hungry. They were exhausted. They were in pain. It was awful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these civilians evacuated to Velepromet at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because very many civilians came from basements, from shelters, from houses where they were, because they knew that the convoy was coming and everybody wanted to get out of that hell. So Dr. Bosanac asked if they could be away from the wounded, if they could stay at Velepromet because the convoy would come there too, so it was mostly women and children who went to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when these civilians were evacuated, or rather transported to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This entire procedure started in the morning and went on until late in the afternoon, and evening between 18th and 19th. A day before the convoy came, they had already reached Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you spend the last night in the hospital, the night before your evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the last night by my husband's side, because he asked for me to be with him during evacuation because immobile, so that I could give him water, whatever else he needed. So I slept by his feet on his bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the condition your husband was in during that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was awful. He was terribly afraid. He was a sportsman and his work also kept him very active, and he simply could not reconcile himself to immobility and depending on someone else and he cried a lot. So he always asked for me to be by him to give him something, to bring him a bit of water, juice or something, but to be next to him and to talk to him because he was terribly frightened as to how he would live after that, in that state, immobile, so I was with him during those last days, all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a medical record with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The morning before we were to be evacuated, Nurse Biba gave every wounded person his medical record, if they were to be transported further, although we had all assumed that we were going to Zagreb, especially the wounded who needed further treatment and further care because our hospital was not in a position to do so, so every patient, every wounded person had his medical record with him so that his treatment would be continued at another hospital. I do not know where. My husband was wounded so badly that he could not hold these papers, this medical record, so it so happened that I took this bag with his medical record and I still have it with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have this record now, here in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you later in 1992 ask two doctors who have treated or had treated your husband in Vukovar to confirm that medical record in two separate letters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. One of the doctors is Dr. Nejarvo and the other is Dr. Aleksijevic, who in the hospital treated my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would now like, your Honours, to show the witness a copy of the record she showed to us in the days before today, and I would like to ask her to tell us whether the copy we have is, in fact, the copy of the original of hers. The Defence is already in possession of this record of both the Croatian original and the English translation, and I have here again copies here of the translation and the original for the judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, are you tendering these documents in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Dosen, is that copy the copy of the original you have with you today in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly, lead us through these pages of the document just referring quickly, what do you see, what do you see written on that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the medical record of my husband's illness. It is a document that says his name and surname, Dosen, Martin, born in 1952, residence, Vukovar, Mose Pijade, sex, male. On 16th November 1991 he was admitted to the Vukovar medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. If you now turn to the second page, and could tell us, not to read everything, but just to tell us in your language what we have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the second page there is an anamnaesis and the medical findings of his wounds and the illness of my husband. It is written in Latin. That is why I asked Dr. Aleksijevic to translate this for me to know what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The third page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third page is a list of my husband's temperature because it was taken every day. That is to say that it is a very important document for me because it says that on the 16th November, the 17th November, and the 18th November, his temperature was taken. On the 19th and 20th it was not. That is when they were being prepared for evacuation. That document is important for me, because it shows that my husband was at the Vukovar hospital and he has never been seen since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could please keep the next pages in your original, because they are empty, they are only forms, and come to the two letters we were referring to earlier. The first letter is a letter by whom, Ms. Dosen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first letter is a certificate by Dr. Juraj Njavro, a surgeon at the Vukovar hospital who treated my husband's leg when he was first wounded and he wrote: "Dosen, Martin, hurt in August, wounded by a grenade. His right leg was wounded. He was treated as an out-patient. He regularly came for check-ups. The certificate is being given at the request of his wife."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can skip the last letter because it confirms just what you have told us; if you agree, Ms. Dosen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am tendering that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: THE REGISTRAR: That will be Exhibit 62 and the English translation, 62A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Ms. Dosen, were you told in the morning of the 20th November that you would be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that day in the morning a soldier in uniform came. He looked special. We did not know who he was then. At least on that occasion he was decent. He said, "I am Major Sljivancanin. From now on I am in command here. We are now going to read out a list of names to you and please, as we call out your name, get out of the hospital".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, briefly, describe to us the appearance of the person you described as, "Sljivancanin"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally think I shall never forget him, particularly because his looks were special. You rarely see such people in our parts, because he is very tall with a big black moustache. You would remember him anyway, if you saw him, and he has a Montenegrin accent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? Were you taken out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to him were two other soldiers whom I do not know, and in their hands they had a list, and they were reading it out. It so happened that my husband, Martin Dosen, was the first on the list and Tadija Dosen, Ivan Dosen, Ivan Vulic and all of them, and they were told to go out as their names were called out. My husband was immobile so I stayed on waiting for him to be transferred from his bed onto a stretcher. So the wounded who could move were walking by me as they were getting out. I still was not aware of what was going on outside. Then two nurses came and they were supposed to carry my husband. However, he was a man who weighed 120 kilos and it was not all that easy to carry him, so it was hard for them so Major Sljivancanin ordered two soldiers to carry him out on a stretcher. When they took him, my daughter and I followed the stretcher and it is only then that I went out in front of the hospital. To my left there were other civilians, women, children, who were already standing out there. I am sorry, on the right-hand side, civilians were on the right-hand side, and at the left-hand side we had to pass by two lines of soldiers that were standing on the left- and the right-hand side but then I realised that we were not moving towards the main entrance, but that we were going behind the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, Ms. Dosen, I have a little problem with my earphones. I cannot really hear any translation. (Pause). Let me just change the earphones, maybe that helps. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now it works again. You are now out of the hospital in the yard of the hospital, and were you then taken further after we have seen these lines of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We had to walk between the two lines and we came to a road behind the Vukovar hospital where four buses were parked, two civilian buses and one military bus and behind it yet another civilian bus. And I saw that my husband was being carried precisely to this military bus which was very unusual to me because if this was a convoy, and if we were all supposed to be evacuated, then how come they were taking him to the military bus? And there were armed soldiers standing next to this bus, four of them outside the bus and two inside. This seemed a bit unusual to me, and not a single wife or child were there. It was only myself and my daughter Tanja who were there. They brought my husband to the bus and they put him next to it because he could not board the bus, because he was incapable of sitting, and they could not carry the stretcher onto the bus. I stood in front of the bus, I looked inside, and then I saw that on that bus it was not two people who were sitting next to each other, two by two, but one by one. Then Ivan, my husband's younger brother and Tadija, my husband's older brother, the young Kozul, Sinisa Glavasevic, I know them all because we grew up together, so I told my husband, "I do not understand this. What is this?", and he said, "I do not understand it too. Something strange is going on here".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were now standing in front of the military bus. Which bus in the line of these buses you saw and you described was this bus? In what position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two buses, one next to another, civilian, normal buses that used to drive us to work or wherever people had to go, but I immediately noticed and I shall never forget, the military bus because I was wondering why a military bus. I turned to a soldier, and I said, "young man, please. Where are these buses going to?", because I saw that it was not a convoy. The European Community was there. No one was there. Only a bit further on Major Sljivancanin was standing by the first bus and issuing orders who was supposed to go where and who was supposed to sit where, and I saw that something was wrong. And he said, "I am sorry, but I really do not know. Ask someone else". At that moment a soldier in uniform from the bus, a reservist, got my younger brother-in-law out, my husband's younger brother, and they pushed him so hard towards the fence of the hospital and said that he should get everything out of his pockets, whatever he had, and he said, "you Ustasha, now we are going to show you", and Martin was lying out there but was looking at this other man with an automatic rifle, was standing there pointing it at him. My daughter started crying, my husband started crying, I did not know what to do, and he said, "do something! Take my child away from here!", and I said, "how do you think I am going to do that? I have a Kalashnikov pointed at my back? How do you think I am going to take her?", and he said, "I do not know what you are going to do, but do something. Take my chain off my neck and take my ring and take off my watch and I promised my ring to my son". I mean, it was awful. I can never forget that and my child can never forget it. I thought that it was all over, that they would kill this youngest brother in front of us all there on. On the other side they were bringing his niece, Ruzica Markobasic, who was pregnant, five months pregnant. They were also pulling her by her fur coat and her handbag and they were throwing her things around, and they were saying, "you whore, you Ustasha whore, where are your pictures, where are your pictures of your husband cutting off children's finger and making necklaces out of them?". These are such banal things. We did not kill anyone, let alone children. On the contrary, we fed them and we gave them food and my husband helped them. I had a restaurant of my own. I gave them milk and food and oil and sugar and if they were fair and honest. They should have said that, that not a single Croat mistreated children there or beat children there, least of all we, the women, Croat women. On the contrary. In my building where I lived, those who lived next door got wheat flour and bread and yeast and everything from me, and my daughter also baked sweets and she gave them to their children. It is not that we would shut ourselves into the room and not give them anything, and this was a very ugly thing because we did not do that to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Ms. Dosen, what happened to the woman you just described, Ruzica Markobasic? Was she led into the bus eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She was also brought there by a young man. He is not from Vukovar, but I would recognise him. And as they were getting onto the bus, he took my hand and he squeezed my hand. I was wondering what it was. Perhaps it was a message or something. He took her on to the bus and automatically, I opened my hand and there were 2,000 Yugoslav dinars in my hand and I said, "sorry, young man, but what do I need this far?", and he said, "madam, you might need this, but she certainly will not any more".

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Dosen. Maybe your Honours, that is a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. So we stand in recess for twenty minutes. (11.05 am) (A short break) (11.30 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show the witness Prosecution exhibit number 43. That is a still picture from the video about the patients in the hospital we have seen the other day: Can you please put it onto the ELMO? Thank you. It is only one picture so I think we can have the lights like this. Ms. Dosen, do you know a person on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know him. This is my husband's nephew, his sister's son Martin Jakubovski Dosen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe him, what is he wearing, what does he look like on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is wearing hospital pyjamas, but as he was wounded, he had a high fever, and he was always cold, so I gave him this pullover that he is wearing. He was wounded in the arm. He had a serious wound. His hand was to be amputated but Dr. Aleksijevic did all he could to save his hand, so that he used screws and surgery to sew it on, and he had an injury of the pelvic bone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarification, what is the colour of the pullover you were just mentioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The pullover is pinkish. You can see that it is a lady's pullover. It was mine, and I gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it is the person on the right side you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This young man with a sling and his hand in a sling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could point to him on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is him. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Ms. Dosen, did you see this person, Mr. Jakubovski that morning, 20th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly on this bench that he is sitting on, we sat there together, gave him a cigarette, because he also smoked, and when they started calling out the names as he was a mobile patient he went out before us. However, when I reached the bus, he was still not there. He was held up somewhere. In the meantime, while I was standing by the bus, another soldier brought him. He stood in front of the bus. He turned around towards me and Tanja, and he said, "bye aunty, and you cousin, take care", and then he boarded the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this person again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was exhumed from Ovcara and buried in Vinkovci. He was 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Darko Vuk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know him personally, because he was a little older than Martin, but he was very bad. I do not know what we did to him, for him to suddenly become such a big Serb. I thought he was a friend, and I asked him, "Darko, could you save any one of mine, my family?", and he looked at me ironically and said, "you Dosens have done a lot of harm so you just keep quiet".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe his appearance that day? What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He was rather arrogant, he behaved like a great liberator. I do not know who he was liberating me from. I thought that if he was a man from Vukovar, a native of Vukovar, I cannot accept that he was in jeopardy because he was not, at least there was no threat from any one of us, and he did not need to liberate me, but I thought that the situation was such that it was not good for us Croats, that the people around us were very arrogant, they were celebrating. There were some who carried Chetnik insignia. They wore long beards. One of them was so brazen as to lick a knife, threatening to slaughter Croats, that is terrible, that is something I never thought would happen. At least I did not expect it from people I grew up with, I went to school with, with whom I went out, that I went to weddings to, and that they should behave in that way now was terrible. I do not know. I will probably never forget that the same Darko would sit in my restaurant on the Danube with my husband. He was a friend of his, and that it should end up like this, I do not know. I thought he would be a man and that he would assist us, but he behaved as a great liberator and he celebrated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we may turn back to your husband, Martin, you said that he was laying on his stretcher in front of the bus. Did you have now a conversation with Sljivancanin with regard to your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since my husband was fearful for our daughter who was 14, the two of us were alone there and he could not help us in any way, then he told me that I should try and do something. So I realised that our locals, the people of Vukovar could not help us so I told my husband, "I am going to go to the major and ask him what I and my daughter were doing there". So I went up to him next to the other bus and I said, "excuse me, may I ask you something?", and he said, "yes, please". I said, "I do not understand what I and my daughter are doing here. There is not a single other woman or child", and he asked me, "are you arrested?". I said, "no. I think it is a convoy that is going to take me out of Vukovar somewhere", and he said, "what are you doing here then?". I said, "I am here because of my husband", and he said, "where is your husband?", and I said, "there he is, next to the bus", and he said, "who is he?", and I said, "he is Martin Dosen"; "oh, Dosen. Why is he not in the bus?". I said, "he cannot, because he is immobile. He is on a stretcher and he cannot get into the bus with the stretcher". He looked at me, turned around and told two soldiers to go back for Martin and to take him back towards the hospital, and that we should follow. While walking I asked him, "excuse me, but what shall I do with my husband's things?", because I thought that since he was in the hospital, he had a long, "dzeta", so he could not wear anything except a pullover and I thought he would be cold and if we get to Zagreb or somewhere else, can I give him his clothes, a change of clothes, and he had a bag with his things inside. He looked at me and he said, "what does he need that for?", so I was surprised. Because I wondered what he was asking me and I said, "I beg your pardon?". Probably he realised that he had indicated that my husband would no longer need those things, and then -- so he corrected himself and said, "who is going to carry those things?". Then I said, "if there is no one to carry them I will carry it", and then I pushed my daughter in front of me and told her to go forward because I just wanted to join the other women and children, because my husband kept telling me that we should always be where there are lots of other people, where everyone is together, because he was afraid they might kill us if we were alone, and he was especially fearful for Tanja. So, I headed towards the other women and children to the left. However, they did not take Martin back into the hospital, they left him there at the entrance to the hospital because for the immobile patients who were on stretchers who did not have a limb or who were wounded so badly that they could not walk, military trucks came to pick them up, and as far as I was able to see, because I bent down and covered my husband up with a blanket and I stroked his face, and I told him, "take care", and we went off, and they were then carried into those trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before you left, as you said, you left your husband, did you ask Sljivancanin, where these buses, the third one especially, the military bus you referred to before was going to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we were talking about those things, I myself reached the conclusion that some kind of execution was pending, because especially that military bus, I heard people saying that it was a bus for liquidation, and then I asked the major, "please excuse me, could you tell me where those buses are going?", and he said, "which bus interests you?", and I said, "my whole family is in the military bus so I am interested in that particular bus", because I saw that soldiers were standing around that bus watching over it. He said, "that bus, that bus will not go far because the people in that bus, darkness will swallow them up in broad daylight".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen one of the persons you saw boarding that bus again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw any one of them again, though we had all hoped and expected that perhaps they were in captivity somewhere because we took with us in that convoy only 74 wounded whom they wanted to take off at Mitrovica. However, we women and children rebelled, would not let them get off, so they went with us to this infirmary where we spent the night and then they drove us on in the morning. But again, we did not want to move on until the wounded joined us, because they told us we could not go to Croatia, that Croatia does not want us, that we would have to go through Orasje, that in Orasje the bridge had been destroyed, that buses cannot go that way. Then we women said, "never mind, we will carry the wounded but we will not leave them there in the infirmary", so we waited for another hour or two, and then the wounded were brought into the convoy and they were the only ones that we took with us from the Vukovar hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have only a few more questions. You just said that you left with those wounded in a convoy. Do you recall about the time this convoy left the Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
