utterances.text: We thought that in the morning at 8 o'clock we would be moving, as they had said. However, later we realised that they had their own list on the basis of which they took away the people, all the men and the wounded from the hospital, because the European Community representatives had still not arrived in the hospital, and those wounded had not been registered. The European Community people came only about 11, and it was then that they started registering the other wounded who were in the hospital and who were evacuated with us so that we set off some time after 11. We passed through the city centre because they told us that we should go to Velepromet, and then from Velepromet, through Bogdanovci to Vinkovci. That was the agreement reached between Dr. Bosanac, the European Community and the liberators. However, when we reached Velepromet they told us that we could not go through Bogdanovci because apparently there were mines there and they could not be held responsible for us, that Croatia did not want us, but that they would take us through Negoslavci to Mitrovica in Serbia. Again, we reacted. We said that we had nothing to do in Serbia, that we wanted to go to Croatia where we belonged, to Zagreb, to any other place, but that we did not want to go to Serbia. However, they had their own plan. In my personal opinion, we realised that they wanted these 74 wounded as well, and that is why they took us to Mitrovica, because most of our people ended up in Mitrovica, Nis, and all over the place. However, those four buses, not one of them ever reappeared again. Only now at Ovcara have they been found where that terrible massacre was carried out, and this is disgraceful. I would forgive them, perhaps, if my husband had taken up arms and if that same Serb had a weapon and if they had shot at one another, but to kill the wounded that cannot defend themselves who have no arms, it is terrible. It is a crime that has to be punished, and I appeal to you on behalf of my husband, my mother, and the children, that they be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Dosen. Just to conclude my examination, I would like you to show a picture of the hospital building and the surroundings, and I would like to ask you, briefly 17 just to show us the locations. That would be Prosecution exhibit number 8. It is the photo album titled, "Vukovar hospital", if I may ask the usher... And if you could, please, show her the fifth picture, picture number five? Yes, that is the very one. Can you please show us where the entrance or rather exit to the hospital building is, where you and your husband on the stretcher were taken out of the building on the morning of November 20th, and please indicate it -- yes -- with a stick.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is the exit just underneath this cover, this roof, and then you go out of the hospital this way, and then you go to the left, and this is the main exit. This is where the women and children were, and the civilians. This is the driveway through which we passed, and on the left- and the right-hand side were soldiers, and then we would pass through this driveway, and reach the street and here is the rear side of the hospital and behind the hospital were the buses, here. (Indicating). The two civilian ones then a military one then another civilian one and then here behind these buildings were the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Dosen. That concludes my examination, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Cross-examination by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason that I will have a few questions is the statement that I have just received from the Prosecutor that was taken from a child here in The Hague in the hotel. I am very sorry that all this happened to you, and believe me, I had no intention to cross-examine you, except to express my condolences. While you were waiting to be taken away by the buses, did you see Ms. Katica Zera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I not know Ms. Katica Zera in person. I have never had any contact with her. I know her now, but there were so many people in the hospital, that we may have come across one another, but I simply did not know her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me the time when you left the hospital, and how much time you spent outside until you boarded the bus and left with the other women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came out of the hospital at 8 o'clock in the morning. All these things that were happening took place during that one and a half to two hours, next to the buses outside the -- behind the Vukovar hospital. Then I went back among the women and children and civilians who were in the hospital, and we all left together through the main exit, the other side, where the convoy was with the European Community and we left with them. This was after 11 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. No re-examination? No. Ms. Dosen, this court is very grateful to you for coming here to testify. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I call Tanja Dosen. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration, please? TANJA DOSEN (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Tanja Dosen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you born? What was your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 10th January 1977.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember on the 6th September of 1995 Mr. Milner from the Office of the Prosecutor came to see you and took from you a statement about the events that occurred in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that the statement was taken down in the English language, and translated back to you in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember at the time being asked to put your signature on the bottom of each page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at this document that I now show you, please? Perhaps it might be given the next number in order, your Honours. There is no translation into the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be number 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you see your signature appearing on the foot of each page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, any objection? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ms. Dosen, where did you spend your life, where you grew up before 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you live there with your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your parents' name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Martin and Ljubica Dosen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1991, I think you would have been about 14 and a half years of age. Is that right? Towards the end of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In January 1995 I was 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, even though you were quite young at the time, do you have a good recollection of the events that occurred in Vukovar, in particular in the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you in Vukovar during the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you with your mother and father during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the latter part of November of 1991, did you have occasion to -- did your father leave you and your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because he was wounded and he was taken to the Vukovar hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just had it pointed out to me that I think -- I do not know whether you said it or whether the translation made an error, but apparently you said you were 15 in 1995. I think you meant 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. 1992. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us how it was that your father became separated from you and your mother in the latter part of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After his second wounding, he was hospitalised for a short period of time, but he came home because there was not enough room at the hospital. When the building was on fire, since the second and fourth floor were burning, he could not take the -- he could not go down by the staircase, he tried to go down by a rope from the third floor balcony and his right hand was in plaster, so he was going down the rope, he fell and he injured his backbone and his arm and he was taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when this was, approximately, that he went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th or 15th November 1991, five or six days before the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you then go to the hospital with your father and mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. My mother and I stayed behind and my father was taken away by some people who were there in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And did you then later go to the hospital? When did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went afterwards when the shelling had subsided a bit. My mother and I went to the hospital then. However, they would not let me come to see my father because they did not want to tell me that he was immobile, so they took me back home and my mother stayed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, did you then later go up to the hospital yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father told my mother that evacuation was to take place from the Vukovar hospital and that we should go back to the Vukovar hospital together, so on 18th we came to the hospital together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you stay when you got to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First we stayed next to my father, but since there was not enough room for sleeping there we were sent to the floor above the basement, but my father would not let my mother leave him, so I went with my granny.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you and your granny staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the basement. That is actually the floor above the basement underneath the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you there with your granny?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed that night and then Dr. Bosanac came and said that, "you cannot stay there", because there were very many people at the hospital because they heard that there would be an evacuation and she said that who wanted to go to Velepromet could go there because there would be a convoy going to Croatia from there too, but then my mother came and said that I should not go because my father would not let us go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I went to see my father and we were waiting there to see what would happen to us. My father was immobile and he wanted my mother and I to help him because there were not enough medical staff available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day the Yugoslav army entered the hospital, and also the reservists, or rather people who lived in Vukovar before, but who were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how could you tell the difference between the Yugoslav army and the reservists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army were mostly young people, and they had five-pointed stars on their caps and reservists were older, unshaven, with long hair. They had four Ss on their caps or cockades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember the date it was when these people came, the JNA and the reservists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do when they came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they came into the hospital they first looked around to see who was there, then they walked around the hospital, they gave some people cigarettes, they provoked other people, especially the locals. Not the Yugoslav People's Army. And after that two soldiers stood at the entrance and did not allow any of the locals to get in any more and what happened after that in the hospital itself and in the room I was, there were not any army people left there. The door was closed and we could not see anything after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then, after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then on the morning of November 20th, a soldier came into the hospital. He had a list, and he was calling out the names of people who were wounded and who were staying at that hospital, saying that they should get out. My father, he was immobile, he was on the first on the list. They could not carry him out because they had to wait for a stretcher to be brought so that they could carry him out, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you with your father at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your mother? Was she there too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother was also there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then two nurses came who were supposed to carry my father. However, they were not strong enough because my father was rather heavy and then two soldiers came and they carried him to the back door of the hospital, to the road. They put him in front of the third bus, which was a military bus, and that is where they left him, and then we stood there and waited, what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did happen next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that in the first two buses, and in the fourth bus they put as many people as they could; however, the third bus was a military bus and only arrested people went into that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people that you saw going into the third bus, did you know any of those people by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because most of them were my relatives. Two brothers of my father, then also two cousins, my aunt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us now the names of any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Dosen, Tadija Dosen, Zvonko Vulic, Josip Kozul, Sinisa Glavasevic, Martinja Dosen, Ruzica Markobasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the next thing to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were standing there, my mother asked a soldier where these buses were going, and he answered that he did not know, but since my father did not have any clothes on, she asked why they did not take him anywhere because it was rather cold, and then a soldier said that a stretcher could not get on the bus. Then they said that they would bring a truck, and Major Sljivancanin ordered a truck to be brought then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Major Sljivancanin. How did you know it was Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Yugoslav army entered the Vukovar hospital, Major Sljivancanin came to the entrance and he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you there when he did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, because my father's bed was the first one by the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what happened next? What was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then first they brought my aunt who was pregnant. They brought her to this third bus and they started searching her, and they threw her things out of her handbag and then a soldier, as he led her into the bus, he put something into my mother's hand and my mother opened her hand and she said, "what is this?". It was money and she said, "why are you giving it to me? I do not need it", and he said, "you might need it and she will never need it again".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your aunty's name, the one that was pregnant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ruzica Markobasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then two soldiers brought Martinja Jakubovski from the hospital in front of the third bus too. He was telling them something. I did not exactly hear what he was saying. I was just asking what was happening and he told me that I should stay calm and that everything would be all right and he boarded the third bus too. They took him into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just look at this photo I show you: I would ask that the photograph be put on the ELMO machine beside you. Could you look now beside you there and do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is my aunt's son, Martin Jakubovski. He was also brought to the third bus and he was identified at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he is the one that spoke to you when you were standing there outside the hospital, that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after Martin Jakubovski-Dosen spoke to you, what was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then my mummy went to Major Sljivancanin and she asked him why my father was not taken away from there. Then he ordered two soldiers to take a stretcher and to take him to the truck, because the stretcher could not get onto the bus, and then my mummy said, "Well, would you take these things too?", and he said, "Well, he will not be needing those things". Then he probably realised what he had said, and then he turned to my mummy and said, "who do you think is going to carry these things of his?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then they put him down because the truck had not arrived yet, and then Major Sljivancanin told me and my mummy that we should join the other women and children. We have never seen him after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father say anything while this was all happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were standing in front of the bus, he told my mummy to get me out of there and did she not see what was going on, and then he took off his wristwatch and he gave my mummy that wristwatch and in the hospital, in Vukovar, on 18th November, he gave me the chain he wore around his neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, when we were sent to join the other women and children, for some time we stood in front of the main hospital building and then we were told to board the buses because the evacuation was starting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you boarded the buses, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we went through the centre of town and we came to Velepromet. We just stood there for perhaps ten or fifteen minutes and then we were taken to Negoslavci. We also stood there for a short period of time and then finally we went to Sremska Mitrovica where we spent a few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after a few days in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we went to Croatia. We went to Jakovo. We only spent a few hours there, then we went to Djurdjovac. We only spent the night there and then mummy and I came to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you seen your father since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never seen him since, and I never heard anything about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what of your cousin, Martin Jakubovski-Dosen. Have you ever heard or seen him since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only when he was buried after having been identified at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your aunty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She has not been identified yet. Nor has she been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I wish to express my condolences, because of the fact that this tragedy occurred, and the only question I have is about the time, if you know, when you went out. Were there other people there, I mean in front of the hospital, women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went out early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot exactly tell, around 7 o'clock, because the European Community arrived only around 11. I know exactly because I had my watch on my wrist and when I boarded the bus I looked at the watch and it was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 11 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 11 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question, at what time did you last see Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what time it was, but I just know that it was on the 19th November, before the evening began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking about the 20th. When did you first see him? You went out at 7 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went out at 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, how much time is needed to get from the basement to the street? Perhaps about 10 or 15 minutes, and then we stood there for about fifteen or twenty minutes when he came, then my mother talked to him. M FILA: So about half an hour, so perhaps around 7.30. Thank you very much and I apologise once again for having questioned you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No questions. Is there any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection. Well, thank you, Ms. Dosen, so much for coming here to testify. You may now be released. I wonder whether the Prosecutor feels that we may be able to hear the next two witnesses before lunch?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure whether they are available, your Honour, but I would certainly call the next witness, and if an enquiry can be made, I am ready to proceed, put it that way, at least with the next witness. They may not be here though, your Honour. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, I would like to ask both parties -- whether they are in a position to provide, whenever possible, to the court a copy, if possible in English, of any international agreement entered into by the Republic of Croatia between, say, June and December 1991. If they happen to know of any such agreement, it would be most helpful to the court. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, we will make enquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you say, "agreement", do you mean agreements with Yugoslavia too, perhaps, or with some other states?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, not only with Yugoslavia, any international agreement. We have already been given an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Agreements with Yugoslavia are in the documents I provided to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness to make the solemn declaration. KATICA ZERA (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Katica Zera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Zera, if you would like to have a drink of water at any time, there is a glass there for you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20th November 1960.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Zera, could you speak up a little bit? I know this is hard for you, so... but just move in a little bit. That is the idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if you would not mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20th November 1960.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bodjani, which is in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you spend the majority of your adult life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- were you married in Vukovar, and I am talking the period prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes I was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your husband's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mihajlo Zera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do for a living? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A driver, a professional driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did he drive for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He drove for Cazmatrans, that is a company, and during the war, because he could not get out of Vukovar, he stayed in the town and the hospital needed a driver, so he took the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he drive? What sort of vehicle did he drive for the hospital? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning it was an ambulance, then a combi-van. It depends. When the vehicles were destroyed, then he drove whatever was left. Civilian or any other vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you and your husband have any children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what children do you have? What were the sexes of the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Boy and a girl. A son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the girl born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the boy born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember your husband's birth date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. 7th August 1955.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some questions about the siege of Vukovar, and picking up at about in September of 1991 through to November 1991, now, during that time, where were you staying when the siege was on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September we came to the hospital because I am a diabetic and I take insulin and my husband worked in the hospital, and they worked all day and all night so he could not take care of us. So he brought us there, and our part of town had fallen. It was under the JNA, so we could not stay in our own house, so we spent all that time in the hospital from September until the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what part of the hospital did he stay in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the old building in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in the hospital, did you come to learn of the fact that there would be an evacuation of the people from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When Vukovar fell, this was the 17th, we heard that there would be an evacuation the next day, but it did not happen. It was postponed, day after day until the 20th, finally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that there was going to be an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps going back to about 18th November 1991, were you still in the hospital at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened? Did anything happen on 18th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the army came. This was the regular army, and after that others came too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say, "the regular army", are you referring to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you determine that they were the Yugoslav People's Army that came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were young, young men, tidy, and they had five-pointed stars on their caps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when they came to the hospital on 18th November what did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They lined up. They were standing there in the corridors. It is hard for me to tell now. And they were outside too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything else of note happen on 18th November, that you can now remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that others also came, as I said. I think that these are paramilitaries, locals from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what made you think that they were paramilitaries as opposed to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On their caps they had four Ss. They were unkempt, beards, long hair, they even had cockades, some of them, and they were older.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they do anything that you could see or remember now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw that they were walking around the corridors, that they were looking at the wounded, and I know that they would recognise them. They would recognise people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was the next thing to happen, after these soldiers had came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some came in, others went out. There was always someone around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can take you to the morning of 20th November, 1991, did you see your husband on that day, on that -- in the morning of that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he would come to fetch us because we were in a small room in the basement. Myself with the children, and another woman with her children, her husband was my husband's colleague. He was also a driver. They told us not to go out until they came to fetch us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of your husband's colleague who was also a driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilija Asazanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time in the morning was it when your husband told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have a watch, and I do not know. I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you then -- did your husband come back as was planned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Both he and Ilija came back to fetch us, and we went out together. We went as far as the exit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got to the exit, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to the door was Major Sljivancanin, and a lot of soldiers. He told us that the men should go to one side and the women and children to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know it was Major Sljivancanin that said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He introduced himself. He delivered a speech. He introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you have a conversation with your husband at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When he said that we should separate my husband stopped for a while. I asked him whether he needed any money. He did not want anything. He just wanted to congratulate me on my birthday because it was my birthday that day, and while we were standing there for a moment, Major Sljivancanin came up and said, "come on, hurry up, you have to separate now".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband and his colleague joined the group that was already there. I just stood and watched, and then we went to the side where the women and children were and we joined them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see your husband after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Never again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We waited for the buses, and after quite some time, I cannot say how long it was, the buses came, and we were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the last day that you saw your husband, can you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He had a sweat suit, a sweater, and a white coat and on his feet he was wearing sports shoes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember whether he had any tattoos on his body at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the tattoos he had on his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had the date when he joined the army, the date when he served in the army, and a heart with an arrow through it. Those were tattoos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he had ever broken a part of his leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not it was the right or left leg? You may not remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember, and when I was giving this statement his mother told me which leg it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I want to you look at a photograph I am about to show you, and might this photograph be placed on the ELMO? I have a copy for Mr. Fila, and it be given the next number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please can that be placed on the ELMO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I tender that, your Honour. Now, after you and your husband separated, the women and children went off in one direction, and your husband went and you did not see him again. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were evacuated in a convoy. We spent one night in Mitrovica in a sports hall. After that we went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make enquiries as to what had happened to your husband after you left, after you arrived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I did. Along the way too in Mitrovica. There were people who had got to the barracks and then they joined us in the convoy. There was Mr. Simunovic, Jakob.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you find out about your husband, as you made these enquiries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not much, just that they got as far as the barracks and the compound there, then they were taken back to the hospital, and all the others stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then? What did -- was that the only thing that you found out about your husband, right up until the present moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not know anything else. I heard in Zagreb from Mr. Simunovic that he had been beaten in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear any more? Did you make any other enquiries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did make enquiries but I did not learn anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila? Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as for the previous witnesses, I wish to express my regrets for what happened. I only have a few questions. Who spoke to you and when about this case among the Tribunal's investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Mira Draskovic. What do you mean, "when"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On behalf of the Tribunal, the Prosecutor's Office. You said that you asked your mother about the leg and who was talking to you? Who was interviewing you and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were filling in a form for a -- a search form in 1992, actually, and they wanted us to describe the body, whether there were any fractures, tattoos, or diseases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We still have not understood one another. Did anyone, on behalf of the Prosecution, come to see you and talk to you and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among the Prosecutors? Yes, they visited us at home and asked us whether we would be willing to testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it? And when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date exactly. I know that Ms. Mira Draskovic was there, and I cannot recall the name of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year was this? Last year? This year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1997, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the identification of my husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign any statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon, I did. Yes. They came to our house and both I and my son signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was last year, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We do not have those statements, your Honour. Especially the son's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So far as I am concerned, neither do we, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you not have one either. Oh. Never mind. Let us continue then, shall we? May I please take you back to the worst day in your life, but I have to do it. I do apologise. How did you leave the hospital on the 20th, all four of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All eight of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am talking about your husband and your two children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were separating from your husband were you still altogether? All four of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went off with the group with the men whereas I and the children went in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would not have asked you if you had not omitted to mention your children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Myself and the children. You see, I stopped for a moment and was looking at the group, my husband and Ilija joining that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The children may have made two steps in the direction of the group in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what time it was when you left, and how much time later did you see Major Sljivancanin, who introduced himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said I did not have a watch at the time. It was the morning. Maybe about 8 o'clock. It may have been before or a few minutes after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not expect you to tell us the exact minute. So it was about 8 o'clock, and it was then that you saw Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came out, so when you came out you saw Sljivancanin straight away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were talking to Sljivancanin, was your son present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, when he was making the speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe they were a step or two away from me. My husband came up to me, he kissed me, he wished me a happy birthday and then Major Sljivancanin came up and said, "there is no hesitating, you have to separate. Each one to his side".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And your two children were there, a metre or two away from you? Thank you very much, and I apologise for having to ask you these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Zera, thank you so much for coming here to testify. I see that there is no objection to the witness being released so she is released. You may be released. Mr. Niemann, do you think we can call the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are not in a position to call the last witness, your Honour, and I think we need to have a discussion with Mr. Fila about another matter, so I think it might be convenient if we could do that. I should indicate that after the conclusion of the next witness we will be making an application in closed session, so if that could be -- I just alert the Registrar to that so that if we could be in that position, so at the conclusion of the next witness, if your Honours please. I am sorry, this witness is not available just at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So we -- Mr. Fila? All right. We stand now in recess until 2.30: 2.15. Is that all right? 2.15? Yes, 2.15. (12.45 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.15 pm) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Stand up, and make the solemn declaration DRAGAN ZERA (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state to the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Zera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in 1991 you were just 13 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to school in Vukovar, and in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a salesperson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the profession of your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professional driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was his employer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked in Cazmatrans and in 1991 he got a job at the Vukovar hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when you left your home and went to live at the hospital in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate what time that was, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17th September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody else from your family move with you to the hospital, or was already there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my mother and my sister went with him -- with me and since my father was already working there he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many nights did you spend at the Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The nights from 17th September until 20th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like now to show you a picture, and that would be Prosecution exhibit number 8. It is again the fifth photograph. Thank you. Dragan, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now explain to us what you have seen on the morning of 20th November 1991 when you were taken out of the hospital, and if you may, you could refer to this picture. That would assist us, and if I may ask you, you have to indicate that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 20th November in the morning we got out here. This is where they separated us from my father. They said that the men should go to the left-hand side and the children and women to the right-hand side, then we were standing here for about two hours, next to the buses. (Indicated). Major Sljivancanin addressed us there. He introduced himself to us and he made a speech. We stood there for some time after that, and then we moved towards the buses that were waiting here. We were sitting on the buses for some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I quickly interrupt you? You said that you were taken out of the hospital and you indicated on the picture the exit. Can you tell us who told you to leave the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers of the JNA army told us to leave the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Sljivancanin. Did you know him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know him until he addressed us and until he introduced himself to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said later that you left your father at the -- close to the exit of the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the exit of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can you tell us the name of your father, and the name also of your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mihajlo Zera and Katica Zera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like now to show you another picture and this is the most recent Prosecution exhibit, I believe it is number 65. Can you tell us who this person is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This picture was taken in 1991 in front of the old Vukovar hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Last question, after you have boarded the buses, where were you taken to? Do you remember the route the buses took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went towards the fairgrounds, next to Velepromet and then we went to Negoslavci where we stood for about half an hour and then we went to Mitrovica. We spent the night there and then we went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So I assume there is no objection to the witness being dismissed. Mr. Zera, thank you so much for coming here to testify. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Prosecutor has anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the evidence that we have available for this week, but we now wish to make a submission in closed session, if the court could go into closed session, your Honours, and my colleague Mr. Williamson will make the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila? Any objection? Any comment? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No thank you, your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we move on to our closed session, may I, for one second, take a few seconds of your time? I would like to take this opportunity to point out that we are now coming to the end of a good week of hard work, and on behalf of my colleagues and myself I would like to express to both parties, to the Defence and the Prosecution our sincere appreciation for their cooperative and helpful attitude. I think it is indeed gratifying to note that we all share the same concern, namely to ensure the accused an absolutely fair, effective and expeditious trial. So thank you so much. I hope that the same atmosphere will continue also in the next weeks. I now suggest that we move to the closed session. (In closed session)
